At a hearing held today, Apple is challenging the UK government's decision to refuse to publicly confirm whether it has issued a request demanding access to users' encrypted data. Details are as follows.

Some background

Earlier last year, The Washington Post reported that the UK government had secretly ordered Apple to build a backdoor into all content uploaded by global users to iCloud.

The order itself is subject to strict confidentiality rules, and Apple is further prohibited from publicly confirming or discussing this request.

The UK government has long maintained a policy of "neither confirm nor deny" the existence of individual orders, and companies that receive such orders are likewise prohibited from disclosing that they have received them.

Reportedly, after receiving but not confirming the order, Apple removed the option for UK iCloud users to enable Advanced Data Protection (ADP).

The reason is that once ADP is enabled, iCloud backups and other categories of iCloud data would be protected by end-to-end encryption. Therefore, Apple would rather choose not to offer ADP to new UK users than comply with the UK's backdoor order—even though the order reportedly applies to global users.

At this stage, Apple's standoff with the UK government has split into two fronts: one is challenging the fundamental request to access encrypted data, and the other is opposing the "gag order" that prohibits it from publicly discussing the request.

In April 2025, a judge rejected the UK government's attempt to keep the basic details of Apple's legal challenge confidential, ruling that disclosure of the case's mere existence would not harm national security.

Several months later, under pressure from the White House, the UK government dropped its request to access US users' data under its secret powers. However, the request has not entirely disappeared: the UK subsequently issued a new notice specifically targeting Apple users located within the UK.

A few weeks later, there were reports that after the original global order was replaced by a new order targeting UK users, Apple had launched a second legal challenge against the UK government.

Speaking of which, that brings us to today's latest developments.

Apple challenges the confidentiality arrangements surrounding the order

According to Reuters, Apple today challenged the UK government's continued refusal to confirm or deny the existence of a new "technical capability notice" at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) in London.

According to Reuters, Apple's representative lawyers argued that the government's confidentiality policy hinders meaningful public discussion of the case and undermines the principle of open justice.

The following are excerpts from the report:

At the hearing held on Thursday at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, Ben Jaffey, a lawyer representing the advocacy groups Privacy International and Liberty, said the government's position had become "absurd." He pointed out that "the truth is already out," meaning the information was already in the public domain. He noted that US politicians and officials had publicly mentioned the original notice, and anonymous UK government sources had also confirmed the matter to the media. Both he and Apple's lawyers argued that the UK government's "neither confirm nor deny" policy is an insult to open justice and prevents the public from having meaningful discussions on the relevant issues.

To clarify, the focus of today's hearing is on the confidentiality arrangements surrounding the order, not the fundamental legal question of whether the UK government originally had the power to demand access to Apple's encrypted data.

After today's hearing concludes, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal will rule on whether the government can continue to adopt its "neither confirm nor deny" policy in this case. According to Reuters, the formal hearing on Apple's challenge to the technical capability notice itself is not expected to take place until after next year.
